title: The Thief Beside Jesus Had No Time Left to Repair His Reputation—Only Enough Time to Receive Mercy
paragraphs: The Thief Beside Jesus Had No Time Left to Repair His Reputation—Only Enough Time to Receive Mercy

He could not undo what he had done. He could not rebuild the life he had destroyed. He could not climb down from the cross and prove that he had changed. All he had left was a dying breath, a guilty past, and Jesus beside him—and somehow, that was enough.
There is something terrifying about running out of time.
Not running late.
Running out.

No tomorrow to fix what happened yesterday. No second career. No restored reputation. No opportunity to return what was taken, repair every relationship, apologize to everyone wounded, or spend the next twenty years proving that you have become a different person.
Imagine knowing that your final chapter has already begun.
Your hands cannot move.
Your feet cannot run.
Your sentence has been pronounced.
People are watching you die.
And whatever reputation you once had is now buried beneath one word:
Criminal.
That was the man hanging beside Jesus.
We are not told his name.

We do not know his childhood. We do not know the face of his mother. We do not know what choices brought him to that cross or how many warnings he ignored before Rome finally drove iron through his existence.
Luke simply identifies the condemned men as κακοῦργοι—kakourgoi—criminals, evildoers.
That is how history meets him.
Not as a misunderstood hero.
Not as a basically good man who made one harmless mistake.
A condemned criminal.
And this matters, because the beauty of this story disappears if we sanitize the man Jesus saved.
Grace becomes cheap sentimentality when sin is made insignificant.
The Gospel does something far more astonishing.
It tells the truth about human guilt...
and then tells an even greater truth about the mercy of Christ.
Three crosses stood at Calvary.
On one cross hung rebellion.
On another hung repentance.
And in the middle hung Redemption Himself.
One dying criminal looked at the crucified Jesus and mocked Him:
“If You are the Christ, save Yourself and us.”
He wanted rescue without surrender.
Deliverance without repentance.
A kingdom without a King.
He wanted Jesus to remove his cross, but there is no indication in Luke’s account that he wanted Jesus to rule his heart.
And then the other criminal spoke.
Listen carefully, because these may have been among the most important words he ever said.
“Do you not even fear God...?”
Then comes the confession that makes this scene so uncomfortable for a culture obsessed with self-justification:
“We indeed justly...”
In Luke’s Greek:
καὶ ἡμεῖς μὲν δικαίως
Kai hēmeis men dikaiōs.
In context: “And we indeed justly...”
He does not blame Rome.
He does not blame his childhood.
He does not compare himself with someone worse.
He does not say, “Everybody makes mistakes.”
He does not rename evil as trauma, weakness, complexity, or circumstance.
He admits guilt.
“We indeed justly, for we are receiving what our deeds deserve.”
Then he looks toward the bleeding Man hanging beside him and says something extraordinary:
“This Man has done nothing wrong.”
Think about that.
A condemned man recognizes the innocence of Jesus while many surrounding Him reject Him.
But he sees more than innocence.
He sees a King.
Jesus has been beaten.
Mocked.
Stripped.
Nailed to wood.
There is no visible palace.
No earthly throne.
No army charging over the hill.
No crown except thorns.
No appearance of victory.
And this dying criminal says:
Ἰησοῦ, μνήσθητί μου...
Iēsou, mnēsthēti mou...
“Jesus, remember me...”
And he connects that plea with Christ’s kingdom.
That is staggering faith.
He looks at a crucified Man...
and sees a coming King.
Everyone else can see nails.
He sees a kingdom.
Everyone else can see humiliation.
He sees royalty.
Everyone else can see apparent defeat.
He believes Jesus still has a future—and somehow dares to ask for a place in it.
“Jesus, remember me when You come into Your kingdom.”
Notice what he does not say.
“Jesus, look at all the good I have done.”
He has no résumé.
“Jesus, give me a few years and I will prove myself.”
He has no years.
“Jesus, let me repair my reputation first.”
Too late.
“Jesus, let me perform enough religious works to balance the scales.”
His hands are nailed down.
He cannot be baptized before his death.
He cannot give money to the poor.
He cannot go on pilgrimage.
He cannot spend decades building a respectable Christian testimony.
He cannot descend from his cross and knock on the doors of everyone he hurt.
He cannot demonstrate a lifetime of subsequent obedience.
He has nothing to offer Jesus as the price of mercy.
Nothing.
Except the empty hands of faith.
And empty hands, strangely enough, are exactly the kind of hands capable of receiving a gift.
Then Jesus speaks.
And if you have ever believed that your past has permanently disqualified you from coming home to God, do not rush past these words.
In the Greek text of Luke 23:43:
Ἀμήν σοι λέγω σήμερον μετ’ ἐμοῦ ἔσῃ ἐν τῷ παραδείσῳ.
Amēn soi legō sēmeron met’ emou esē en tō paradeisō.
“Truly I tell you, today you will be with Me in paradise.”
Read the heart of that promise again.
σήμερον — sēmeron.
Today.
μετ’ ἐμοῦ — met’ emou.
With Me.
ἐν τῷ παραδείσῳ — en tō paradeisō.
In paradise.
The criminal asked Jesus to remember him.
Jesus promised him presence.
He asked for mercy sometime in the coming kingdom.
Christ answered with something breathtaking:
Today.
With Me.
Paradise.
Jesus did not pretend the man was innocent.
The man himself had already admitted the opposite.
Jesus did not rewrite his earthly history by pretending his crimes never happened.
He did something infinitely greater.
He rewrote his eternity.
That is grace after ruin.
And maybe this is where the story stops being about an unnamed criminal two thousand years ago.
Maybe this is where it finds you.
Because some people reading this are carrying things nobody around them knows.
There are photographs you hope nobody ever sees.
Messages you wish you had never sent.
Relationships you destroyed.
Promises you broke.
Money you wasted.
Years you cannot recover.
Secret addictions.
Private compromises.
A marriage wounded by your choices.
Children you failed.
Parents you dishonored.
People you betrayed.
Bodies you used.
People who used you.
A faith you abandoned.
A season when you knew exactly what God was telling you...
and chose the opposite.
Perhaps everybody around you thinks you are doing fine.
But you know.
And sometimes, late at night, the prosecutor in your mind opens the old files.
Remember this?
Remember her?
Remember him?
Remember what you did?
Remember what you became?
Remember how many times God warned you?
And eventually shame whispers its most poisonous sentence:
“Jesus might forgive people...
but surely not people like you.”
Look at the cross.
There is literally a man dying beside Jesus whose life is already beyond earthly repair.
He cannot rehabilitate his public image.
He cannot construct a respectable Christian future before coming to Christ.
He cannot earn his way into paradise.
And Jesus does not say:
“Too late.”
Jesus does not say:
“Your record is too long.”
Jesus does not say:
“Clean yourself up and then come back.”
Jesus does not say:
“Convince Me that you deserve another chance.”
The guilty man turns toward Christ in repentance and faith...
and mercy meets him before death does.
This does not mean repentance is unnecessary.
The thief demonstrates the opposite.
He stops defending himself.
He acknowledges that his judgment is deserved.
He recognizes Jesus’ innocence.
He appeals personally to Jesus.
He recognizes Christ’s kingdom.
He entrusts his dying future to the crucified King.
Grace did not teach him that sin did not matter.
Grace taught him where a guilty sinner must go.
To Jesus.
This is why biblical grace is so scandalous.
Religion constructed around human merit says, “Become worthy, then perhaps you can approach.”
The Gospel announces that sinners who could never make themselves worthy are invited to come to the worthy Christ.
We are not saved because our past becomes impressive.
We are saved because Jesus is sufficient.
We are not justified because we finally accumulate enough evidence for our defense.
Scripture says that God justifies the ungodly who believe.
We are not redeemed because we managed to erase every stain.
We are redeemed because Christ shed His blood for sinners.
The thief had no time left to build a testimony.
Jesus became his testimony.
He had no time to repair his reputation.
Jesus became his righteousness.
He had no future achievements to present.
Jesus became his hope.
He could not come down from his cross.
So Christ carried salvation all the way to him.
And here is where we must be careful.
The thief on the cross is not permission to deliberately postpone repentance.
Nobody reading this has been promised a final hour in which repentance will suddenly become convenient.
Scripture says, “Today, if you hear His voice, do not harden your hearts.”
The thief proves that it is never too late while breath remains to turn to Christ.
He does not prove that it is safe to wait.
Those are very different messages.
Do not gamble eternity on another tomorrow.
If Christ is confronting your heart today, answer Him today.
You do not need a polished prayer.
The criminal did not have one.
You do not need theological vocabulary impressive enough to make heaven listen.
He simply cried:
“Jesus, remember me.”
Maybe your prayer tonight sounds more like:
Jesus...
I have sinned.
I have stopped making excuses.
I cannot undo what I have done.
I cannot save myself.
I believe You are the crucified and risen Lord.
I believe You died for sinners.
Have mercy on me.
Forgive me.
Take what remains of my life.
I surrender to You.
Remember me.
Save me.
And understand this clearly: words themselves are not magic.
Jesus saves.
Christ is not a religious formula to repeat while clinging stubbornly to sin.
The Gospel calls us to repentance and faith—to turn from sin and entrust ourselves to Jesus Christ.
The thief had almost nothing left.
But what remained, he turned toward Jesus.
Maybe that is what you need to do now.
Not when your addiction disappears.
Not when your marriage is fixed.
Not when everybody respects you again.
Not after you have attended church long enough to stop feeling ashamed.
Not when you finally feel worthy.
Come guilty.
Come exposed.
Come tired.
Come ashamed.
Come with the wreckage.
But come to Christ.
Because the cross was never erected for people who could save themselves.
And please hear this distinction.
Coming to Jesus does not guarantee that every earthly consequence disappears.
Grace does not always restore a ruined reputation overnight.
Forgiveness does not necessarily erase prison sentences, broken trust, financial consequences, wounded relationships, or the long process of restitution and reconciliation.
The thief was forgiven...
and he still died on his cross.
That matters.
Jesus did not promise him freedom from every temporal consequence.
He promised something infinitely greater:
“You will be with Me.”
Sometimes Christ changes your circumstances.
Sometimes He gives you grace to face the consequences of what you have done.
But forgiveness means your consequences no longer have the authority to define your eternal destination.
Your worst chapter does not get the final sentence.
Jesus does.
That is the heartbeat of everything we mean when we say:
Not that scandal becomes good.
Not that sin becomes irrelevant.
Not that accountability disappears.

But that Jesus Christ is able to take a genuinely guilty human being, bring that sinner to repentance, wash away guilt through His saving work, and write grace where condemnation appeared to have written the ending.
Because Jesus rewrites everything.
Perhaps you know someone who desperately needs to hear this.
Someone who thinks abortion put her beyond mercy.
Someone who thinks adultery became his permanent identity.
Someone in prison who thinks society's sentence must also be God's final sentence.
Someone recovering from addiction who cannot stop remembering who they were.
Someone who abandoned their family.
Someone who walked away from church.
Someone who has spent years pretending not to care about God because admitting how desperately they need Him feels too painful.
Someone who says, “You don't know what I've done.”
Send this to them.
And if this story exposed something you have been hiding, you do not have to tell strangers every detail. But you can stop pretending before God.
There may come a night when your past gets loud again.
Read it then.
Read Luke 23:39–43 again.
Remember the dying criminal.
Remember the dying Savior.
Remember that the guilty man had no achievements left to offer...
and remember who spoke the final word.

Your support helps us keep producing and sharing biblical content intended to point people toward Jesus Christ, repentance, grace, forgiveness, redemption, and transformed lives. Supporting Gospel work should never replace giving to your local church, caring for your family, serving people in need, or obeying Christ personally.
Come to Jesus.
The merchandise cannot save you.
A ministry cannot save you.
A church building cannot save you.
Your reputation cannot save you.
Your good works cannot erase your guilt.
Jesus Christ saves.
And that is why the man beside Him still speaks without having written a single book, preached a single sermon, built a single ministry, or lived one respectable Christian year after his conversion.
His final moments became a monument to grace.
He entered that day condemned by Rome.
He ended it promised paradise by Christ.
He began the scene with nothing in his hands.
He left it with Jesus' word over his eternity.
His reputation could not be repaired.
His crimes could not be undone.
His remaining minutes could not become decades of restitution.
But there was enough time to look toward Jesus.
Enough time to stop defending himself.
Enough time to confess the truth.
Enough time to recognize the King.
Enough time to ask for mercy.
And enough mercy in Jesus to save him.
So when your past whispers, “Look what you did,” look toward the cross and remember what He did.
When shame says, “You are disqualified,” remember the criminal beside Christ.
When the enemy tells you that your story is already finished, remember that there was once a dying man whose final chapter looked like absolute ruin...
until Jesus spoke.
And perhaps that is the sentence your heart needs to carry tonight:

When you have no time left to repair your reputation, no strength left to defend your record, and nothing left to offer God, you may finally discover that Jesus was never asking you to purchase mercy—He was calling you to receive it.
Because somewhere tonight, someone thinks they have gone too far.
Someone thinks Jesus would turn away if He knew everything.
Someone believes the ruins are the ending.
But the criminal beside Jesus leaves us with a different picture.
A cross.
A confession.
A King.
A promise.
Paradise.
The world may remember the scandal that brought you to the cross, but when a repentant sinner turns to Jesus, grace can write an ending shame never saw coming.
